title: Got Regrets Yet? Teachers and the Four Types of Regret
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
source: Dave Stuart Jr. on Substack, December 16, 2025
summary: Stuart maps Dan Pink's four types of regret (Foundation, Boldness, Moral, Connection) onto his Five Key Beliefs (Credibility, Value, Effort, Efficacy, Belonging), arguing that regret is diagnostic information about what teachers value most: helping students learn. Foundation regrets reveal wishes to build stronger systems and expertise, Boldness regrets signal curriculum risks left untaken, Moral regrets expose moments when hurried judgment betrayed core values, and Connection regrets point to unattended relationships. Stuart offers Pink's three-step process for turning regret into action: relive it briefly, reframe it as learning about what you value, and extract one concrete change for the next term, positioning regret as a forward-facing signal rather than self-flagellation.
points: Regret is not rumination; it is information about what you value and what you want to change next.
The four types of regret (Foundation, Boldness, Moral, Connection) appear in predictable shapes in teaching, making them visible and actionable before the end-of-year fog sets in.
Pink's three-step process (relive, reframe, extract and apply) turns regret into a diagnostic signal for which of your Five Key Beliefs you most want to strengthen.
quotes: Regret isn’t just a rumination. Used well, it’s a source of information. It tells us what we value, what we wish we had done differently, and, most usefully, what we want to do now.
Dan Pink, in his book The Power of Regret, identifies four types of regret that cut across cultures: Foundation regrets, Boldness regrets, Moral regrets, and Connection regrets.

Foundation regrets come from failing to do the slow, unglamorous work that sets a person up for long-term flourishing. For teachers, this often looks like systems not built, habits not formed, subject expertise not deepened.

Boldness regrets come from playing it safe when a braver choice was available. For teachers, this might mean the unit we didn’t try, the discussion we chickened out of, the project we shrank to fit our comfort zone.
Moral regrets come from moments when we acted against our values, even briefly. A sharp word to a struggling student, a rushed judgment in a parent email, a corner cut on a colleague who needed us.

Connection regrets come from relationships left unattended. The student we never quite got through to, the co-worker we meant to thank, the kid who slipped through the cracks while we were busy with the louder ones.
Pink offers a simple three-step process: relive the regret briefly, reframe it as information about what you value, then extract and apply a single concrete change.

Our regrets, handled well, become the coordinates for the next chapter. They point us toward the Credibility, Value, Effort, Efficacy, and Belonging we most want to build next.” Archived from Dave Stuart Jr. on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
